documents.abstract: The use of rubrics in Higher Education has become established as a key strategy for improving learning assessment by providing clear criteria, promoting transparency, and facilitating student self-regulation. The incorporation of ICT has enabled their evolution expanding their possibilities for use and analysis, although it has also raised concerns related to privacy and data security when online environments are used. In this context, the design of automated assessment instruments capable of functioning offline is proposed in order to guarantee the protection of students’ information. Based on a literature review, a proposal is developed using spreadsheets, for the creation of two types of rubrics: one focused on grading and another aimed at generating feedback. Automation is achieved through the use of formulas, macros, and Visual Basic programming, making it possible to streamline the assessment process and reduce teachers’ workload. Furthermore, the integration of artificial intelligence through prompting techniques facilitates code generation, the expansion of comments, and the improvement of feedback writing, increasing its personalization and coherence. These tools make it possible to build more efficient, adaptive, and secure assessment systems, although they require an adequate level of teachers’ digital competence. The possibility of integrating both rubrics into a single system and exploring solutions that combine the advantages of offline environments with guarantees for data management in digital settings are proposed as future lines of development.

Introduction Independent music practice depends on learners’ self-regulated learning (SRL), yet how digital tools and artificial intelligence (AI) support the forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases of the SRL cycle, and when such support may undermine learner autonomy, remains unclear. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO through March 2026. Sixteen empirical studies met the inclusion criteria and were appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Because of methodological heterogeneity, we conducted a thematic synthesis rather than a meta-analysis. Results Three categories emerged: traditional digital tools, discriminative AI, and generative AI. Traditional tools supported planning and reflection; discriminative AI enabled real-time error detection; and generative AI may help learners manage task difficulty and translate expert feedback into actionable steps. Study quality was uneven, and several findings came from small-sample or cross-sectional designs, which limits causal inference. Two potential risks, over-scaffolding that may diminish autonomy and visual feedback that may divert attention from sound, were insufficiently studied. Discussion Digital and AI tools appear to scaffold different phases of SRL, but learner autonomy should remain at the core. Fading explicit support and pedagogical guidance may help reduce dependence. Longitudinal studies are required to test these mechanisms.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This multidisciplinary study explores how children interact with a low-cost robotics educational tool designed to teach machine learning (ML) concepts through hands-on making. Artificial intelligence (AI) and ML are increasingly integrated into K-12 education, yet tangible approaches are not extensively studied. We conducted three researcher-led interventions with children aged 10, 11 and 13, each tasked to build an AI-enhanced robot using the robotics kit. Interventions were analyzed both qualitatively and with process mining methods to gain an in-depth view of the interactions. Findings indicate that designing and building were very central throughout the interventions, with the affordances guiding the design process forward. Children exhibited emerging data-driven thinking and ownership of their design process, while still requiring tailored scaffolding throughout the design process. We identify a general structure of the design process from all the interventions and emphasize the importance of building and designing activities. This study provides a new methodological lens to analyzing the interactions between children and embodied AI-educational tools while also contributing to the current body of knowledge on designing and effectively leveraging embodied learning tools.

The advent of the Fourth Industrial Revolution, or Industry 4.0, brings to the fore various opportunities for organisations to globalise with more efficient ways of implementing processes, from customer relations through artificial intelligence to the automation of production. This article presents a desktop review exploring the influence of generational factors on employee talent management, aiming to develop a cybernetic theory to account for autopoiesis. Framed through cybernetics and person–environment theory, this manuscript focuses on the tenets of systemic behavioural and communication patterns constituting generational cohorts subsumed by Generation Z, Generation X, Generation Y, and Baby Boomers, with specific reference to the global and South African context. Leadership should potentially account for generational feedback loops that influence organisational non-purposeful drift to sustain governance. A heightened awareness of generational cultures influencing communication and behavioural patterns may allow leaders to better manage key personnel and potentially optimise resource pooling and feedback loops within the system to retain organisational integrity and promote organisational autopoiesis during future world of work disruptions and uncertainty.

The Internet of Things (IoT) connects physical objects through sensors, embedded processors, and communication interfaces. These devices can collect and share data, helping systems respond automatically to changing conditions. This review offers a structured overview of IoT’s development, enabling technologies, practical applications, and the challenges that affect reliable deployment. It draws primarily on a review article by Yalli, Hasan, and Badawi, which explores IoT’s evolution and its connections to wireless sensor networks, cloud and edge computing, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and blockchain. The paper follows the flow of a typical IoT system, from sensing and communication to data processing and action. It discusses applications in smart homes, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, education, and energy management, as well as practical challenges such as limited device resources, network delays, compatibility between systems, privacy, cybersecurity, and maintenance.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background The vaginal discharge is a common clinical presentation associated with diverse infectious and microbiota-related conditions. Existing artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostic approaches have predominantly focused on detection of individual pathogens and have rarely integrated microbiota-associated conditions within a diagnostic framework. We developed an explainable deep learning framework for automated analysis of Gram-stained vaginal smear images acquired using handheld smartphones or tablets positioned over a conventional light microscope eyepiece. Methods The framework integrates object detection with image-level classification, termed detection-based image classification, to identify diagnostically relevant microscopic structures without requiring exhaustive enumeration of all objects. Five diagnostic categories included vulvovaginal candidiasis (VVC), bacterial vaginosis (BV), trichomoniasis (TV), gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis (GU), and healthy vaginal condition (HL). YOLOv26, RT-DETR and EfficientDet0 were independently trained and evaluated using 1,966 microscopic images comprising 11,069 annotated diagnostic objects. Model explainability and computational benchmarking were assessed. The localization quality was independently evaluated by eight clinicians and microbiologists. Results Class-specific analysis demonstrated that TV and GU consistently achieved the highest detection performance across all models (mAP50 = 0.622–0.752), whereas RT-DETR demonstrated superior performance for VVC, BV, and HL. Expert evaluation showed favorable localization, with Good/Excellent ratings in 84.8 and 85.1% of valid evaluations for YOLOv26 and RT-DETR, respectively, with no significant difference between models (OR = 0.97; 95% CI, 0.58–1.61; p = 0.895). Conclusion This study presents an accurate and clinically interpretable framework that integrates microbiota-associated conditions and sexually transmitted infections for differential diagnosis of vaginal discharge using conventional light microscopy. By linking image-level predictions to localized diagnostic morphology, the framework provides human-verifiable AI evidence as a proof-of-concept prototype. While promising for low-cost implementation, rigorous prospective multi-center validation is required before broad clinical deployment or autonomous diagnosis.

A building consists of many components, each with its own financial impact. A clear evaluation of these impacts is possible through the analysis of the components that make up construction costs. This study aims to evaluate and interpret the combined use of construction cost components for different scenarios using machine learning models. For this purpose, the Extreme Gradient Boosting, Light Gradient Boosting Machine, and Shapley Additive Explanations algorithms were applied. Additionally, the Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithm was enhanced using the Grid Search and Random Search optimization algorithms. Specifically, the model developed with Extreme Gradient Boosting using the Grid Search method increased model performance. Performance metrics such as R-Squared, Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency, Mean Absolute Error, Root Mean Square Error, and Mean Absolute Percentage Error were used for the numerical evaluation of the results. With the help of optimization techniques, the artificial intelligence model was improved by rates ranging from 1.5 percent to 5 percent based on these performance metrics. As a result, the study demonstrates that different representations of the same construction data can influence both prediction performance and model interpretability. A novel scenario-based framework was developed by grouping input variables into Height, Architectural, and Structural feature categories and reintroducing their aggregated representations into the prediction models. The proposed framework contributes to the planning of accurate cost estimates and more efficient resource utilization by providing insights into how alternative feature-grouping strategies affect both construction cost prediction performance and explainable machine learning interpretations.

This study examined the serial mediating role of psychological well-being and self-confidence in the relationship between intrinsic religious motivation and athlete motivation. The study addresses a theoretical and empirical gap in the literature by explaining how religiosity-based spirituality is associated with motivational processes in athletes through a holistic serial mediation model encompassing multiple psychological mechanisms. A cross-sectional correlational survey design was employed. The sample consisted of 401 athletes (118 female, 283 male; M_age = 22.98 ± 4.8) actively competing in various sports disciplines across different regions of Turkey, each with a minimum of five years of licensed athletic experience. Data were collected using the Intrinsic Religious Motivation Scale, the Psychological Well-Being Scale, the Self-Confidence Scale, and the Intrinsic Motivation Scale. Serial mediation analysis was conducted using Hayes’s PROCESS macro (Model 6) with 5000 bootstrap resamples. The results indicated that intrinsic religious motivation was positively associated with psychological well-being (β = 0.221, p < 0.001) and self-confidence (β = 0.229, p < 0.001). Psychological well-being was positively associated with both self-confidence (β = 0.252, p < 0.001) and motivation (β = 0.307, p < 0.001), while self-confidence was positively associated with motivation (β = 0.141, p = 0.005). The total effect on motivation was significant (c = 0.171, p < 0.001); however, the direct effect became non-significant when mediators were included (c′ = 0.063, p = 0.194), revealing an indirect-only mediation pattern. All three specific indirect effects were significant: through psychological well-being (B = 0.060), through self-confidence (B = 0.029), and through the serial pathway (B = 0.007). These findings suggest that intrinsic religious motivation is associated with athlete motivation not directly but via the indirect pathways through psychological well-being and self-confidence.

Regeneration encompasses a variety of processes across biological, urban, and technological domains. This chapter explores the theories, types, and future prospects of regeneration, emphasizing physiological regeneration, urban regeneration through smart technologies, and the potential of regenerative medicine. By synthesizing recent literature, this study aims to provide a comprehensive overview of regeneration’s multifaceted nature and its implications for sustainable development. This chapter reviews existing theories and methodologies, highlighting the importance of regeneration in various contexts, and presents a comprehensive exploration of regeneration, beginning with its historical and conceptual underpinnings and extending into its molecular, genetic, and clinical dimensions. We discuss the major theoretical frameworks that explain regenerative mechanisms, including epimorphosis, morphallaxis, compensatory regeneration, and stem cell-mediated models, alongside concepts like positional information and cellular reprogramming. These theories offer insights into how organisms orchestrate cellular and molecular responses to injury or tissue loss. The types of regeneration are classified based on organismal diversity, underlying mechanisms, tissue-specific regeneration, and distinctions between natural and artificially induced regeneration. Emphasis is placed on the molecular and genetic pathways—such as Wnt, Hedgehog, BMPs (Bone Morphogenetic Proteins), FGFs (Fibroblast Growth Factors), and Notch signaling—that regulate cell proliferation, differentiation, and tissue patterning. Furthermore, the role of stem cells, non-coding RNAs, and immunological responses in shaping regenerative outcomes is analyzed. Advances in regenerative biotechnology, including CRISPR gene editing, 3D bioprinting, organoids, and biomaterials, have brought new promise to regenerative medicine. Clinical applications such as stem cell therapy and tissue engineering are transforming therapeutic strategies for conditions once considered irreversible. Nevertheless, challenges remain in translating laboratory success to human treatment, owing to biological, technical, and ethical limitations. Looking ahead, the integration of synthetic biology, artificial intelligence, and personalized medicine is poised to redefine the future of regenerative science. This chapter concludes by highlighting emerging trends and the interdisciplinary approaches driving the field forward. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of regeneration holds the key to revolutionizing healthcare, offering hope for recovery in degenerative diseases, traumatic injuries, and organ failure.

The chapter addresses how technology, especially such smart tools as smartphones and artificial intelligence, enable women to get more opportunities and influence in different spheres, such as politics, education, and economics. It points out the transformative possibilities of technology in developing nations, as well as makes use of theories like the Diffusion of Innovation Theory to explain how those types of innovations may enable women to become independent and active in fields such as education, financial awareness, and online entrepreneurship. Women have attained access to education, healthcare, finance, and entrepreneurship with the aid of technology, but issues of lack of access, affordability, and cultural limitations continue to be challenging. There are also concerns on online safety and cybersecurity. The chapter highlights that women can be empowered by smart technology, as long as there are equal policies, better digital infrastructure, and improved technological literacy. Social media platforms and e-commerce tools have further opened new avenues for women to participate in economic activities, network with peers, and raise their voices on gender-related issues, contributing to both social and political empowerment. However, the digital gender divide remains a serious concern, as women in rural and low-income settings continue to face barriers related to device ownership, internet connectivity, and digital skills that prevent them from fully benefiting from technological advancements. Inclusive development requires equal access to technology, and there should be a sustained effort by governments, civil society, and the private sector to ensure that no woman is excluded from the prospects presented by the digital revolution.

The contrast in technological trajectories between East and West has stimulated debates about the reasons for such differences since the proposal of the Movius Line in the 1940s. We rephrase the East–West contrasts from ergonomic and functional perspectives: (1) the long-lasting use of handheld tools in the East versus the emerging use of hafted tools in the West around the early Middle Pleistocene or later, and (2) stone-tipped hunting tools were becoming popular in the West during the Middle Stone Age/Middle Paleolithic, whereas they were nearly absent in the East before the Late Paleolithic. By evaluating the impacts of hafting technology and stone-tipped weapons on the morphology and structure of lithic parts, we consider that they may have initiated a new technological path based on hafting. We propose that the scarcity of hafting technology, especially hafted hunting tools, may help explain the limited advances in lithic technology in the East.

Literature on implementing PBL, PjBL, and service-learning approaches in Islamic Religious Education to strengthen empathy and social action remains very limited. This study aims to analyze and synthesize the effectiveness of PBL, PjBL, and service-learning in Islamic Religious Education to sustainably strengthen students' empathy and social action. This study uses a qualitative approach through a PRISMA-based Systematic Literature Review (SLR), drawing on secondary data from Scopus (2019–2026). Results: The PBL model transforms passive religious learning into active cognitive engagement, trains critical legal reasoning (ijtihad), and collaboratively addresses global sustainable development issues. The PjBL model effectively provides an applicable, engaging approach to foster tolerance in multi-ethnic and multi-religious classrooms, ecological awareness, inclusivity, and social harmony within the school environment. Meanwhile, the service-learning approach successfully strengthens the affective dimension, ethical commitment, local cultural wisdom, pesantren character building, and students' real-world praxis through direct community service. Conclusion: These three learning models effectively transform Islamic Religious Education into a medium for strengthening students' deep empathy and tangible social action. This study enriches the literature on Islamic education and serves as a practical guide for developing action-oriented Islamic Religious Education curricula.

Human communication is inherently multimodal, conveying intent not only through linguistic and vocal cues but also through visual signals. However, existing conversational systems have mainly focused on text or speech, leaving out the visual feedback that is essential for natural interaction. In this paper, we propose JAVIS, an end-to-end streaming framework for real-time audio-visual conversational agents. Our key idea is to let the voice and the face speak from a single representation. On top of a shared LLM, a Joint Refined Head produces a unified audio-visual representation, which is fed into dedicated streaming branches for speech and face generation. This end-to-end design avoids intermediate bottlenecks, enabling real-time generation while keeping speech and face tightly synchronized. In addition, we present JAVIS-Syn, a 334-hour synthetic corpus designed to address the lack of expressive audio-visual dialogue data, covering emotionally rich multi-turn conversations and assistant-style exchanges. Experiments show that JAVIS achieves approximately 200$\times$ lower initial latency than a strong baseline, while outperforming baselines in lip synchronization and facial expression appropriateness.

Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3-4B-Base on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science across five frontier and open-weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per-theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR.

When language-model agents operate physical or cyber-physical systems through tool interfaces, do they verify what an interface is really connected to before taking an irreversible action? Current safety alignment evaluates harm primarily within the semantic framing of the user prompt rather than the physical consequence of the backend action channel. We introduce Mirror Lab, a deterministic, replay-verified benchmark that pairs harmless-looking "toy" game interfaces with isomorphic simulated real-world backends across two embodied domains: aerial payload delivery (drone-rescue) and robotic manipulation (robot-arm). Using a progressive five-rung Cue Ladder—which incrementally leaks real-world tool names, physical mass or force magnitudes, irreversibility warnings, and live human telemetry clues into the toy interface—we evaluate three models across 86 episodes (gemma-4-31b-it, gpt-5.6-luna, and claude-sonnet-5.5). We find that: (1) under pure semantic reimagining (pure_toy), all models execute the harmful physical trajectory in 100% of completed episodes while reporting a post-episode belief that the environment was a simulation; (2) cue sensitivity is strongly domain-asymmetric—gpt-5.6-luna and gemma-4-31b-it exhibit a 100% failure rate across every rung of drone-rescue (even when status telemetry reveals 14 human heat signatures beneath a 20 kg drop), yet halt on robot-arm once surgical blade cues (cue_payload) or biometric pulse cues (cue_clue) appear; and (3) models can exhibit epistemic-action dissociation, recognizing in post-hoc probes that a backend was real only after completing the irreversible action.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background and Objectives: Ionizing radiation is essential in diagnostic and interventional medicine; however, occupational exposure may pose health risks to healthcare personnel. Adequate knowledge and appropriate protective practices are essential for minimizing unnecessary exposure. This study evaluated the knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) of specialists, fellows, residents, technologists, and radiographers regarding radiation safety and occupational radiation exposure. Methodology: A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted at the Pakistan Kidney and Liver Institute, Lahore, from 19 June 2025 to 20 November 2025. A structured, self-administered questionnaire comprising eight domains assessed demographic characteristics, radiation-safety knowledge, occupational safety and protective equipment, dosimeter practices, attitudes and perceptions, misconceptions, radiation legislation and dose-related knowledge, and recommendations for improving workplace safety. Of 86 questionnaires distributed, 56 valid responses were received (response rate, 65.1%). Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26.0 and summarized using frequencies and percentages. Results: Among the 56 respondents, 37 (66.1%) were male and 19 (33.9%) were female. Twelve (21.4%) were classified as Category-A radiation workers and 16 (28.6%) as Category-B, while 28 (50.0%) did not report a radiation-worker category. Overall, 45 (80.4%) correctly recognized the cumulative effects of radiation exposure, while 50 (89.3%) recognized that pregnancy does not eliminate the need for appropriate radiation-safety precautions. Forty-one (73.2%) reported always using dosimeters, and 36 (64.3%) reported always maintaining distance from the radiation source during imaging. Forty-one (73.2%) correctly identified the ALARA principle, and 48 (85.7%) identified the Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority as the relevant regulatory body. Important gaps were identified in knowledge of dose-related concepts and selected radiation-protection practices. Conclusion: The findings indicate generally satisfactory knowledge in several core areas of radiation safety but important gaps in selected knowledge domains and workplace practices. Structured and periodic radiation-safety education, regular workplace audits, appropriate dosimeter use, and improved access to ergonomically suitable protective equipment may strengthen radiation-safety practices. The findings also provide a basis for a subsequent institutional educational intervention and re-survey as a quality-improvement initiative.

When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.

This research highlights the need to incorporate the teaching and learning of artificial intelligence, particularly big data, into the educational process. In addition to developing digital literacy, students must acquire knowledge of the technological tools required by companies, which may become their future sources of employment. Furthermore, this research explores the practical application of big data in the world of work.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development

documents.abstract: Who decides what counts as “correct” or standard language today? Correcting language has always been an act of authority. This authority seems now to be quietly shifting toward large language models (LLMs), because they are routinely consulted for proofreading in educational, academic, and professional contexts, valued for the apparent ease with which they produce standardized, well-formed texts. However, which linguistic norm these models draw on when “correcting” language remains underexplored. This is a critical issue, because less linguistically informed users are more likely to accept AI-generated corrections uncritically. In this paper, we examine such corrections and argue that treating LLMs as de facto norm authorities with regard to standard language is premature. We first rethink standard language as a sociolinguistic concept that is negotiated among linguists, norm authorities, model speakers/writers, and codifiers (authors of dictionaries, grammars etc.) rather than a fixed property of a language. We then illustrate LLMs' performance in proofreading empirically, by submitting a German text containing 13 targeted morphosyntactic phenomena for grammar correction to six LLMs (eight model configurations) at three time points. Expectedly, results show variability both between and within models over time, as well as some consistency and several discrepancies with codification and model texts. LLMs, we conclude, may be reasonably reliable for some morphosyntactic variables, and they could be treated as an autonomous norm authority if they can be shown to draw transparently on knowledge codified by reliable sources.

Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

Soft porous crystals can undergo guest-induced structural transitions producing unconventional adsorption isotherms, which are valuable for gas separation and storage applications. However, the evidence for these transitions is scattered across the literature in narrative form and has not been aggregated. Here we use a large language model pipeline to mine the literature for anomalous adsorption, extracting phase-transition events together with material, adsorbate, temperature and pressure metadata and classifying each into an established behavioural class. Benchmarked against human annotation, the extraction stage attains an F1 score of 0.96. When applied at scale, the pipeline yields a curated corpus of 547 transitions across 240 distinct materials, drawn from 200 of 4,252 screened publications, which we further link to crystallographic structures. Analysis of this database shows that the principal behavioural classes, gate-opening and breathing, are distinguished by their functional response. Gate-opening frameworks transform at a significantly lower pressure than breathing frameworks (p = 3.8E-3). In contrast, no difference in pore size, void fraction, linker chemistry or metal identity was detected between the classes. Our findings argue for a functional rather than purely structural description of responsive porous materials. They also highlight the need for a community database that records the guest, temperature and pressure of every reported transition of these materials.

ABSTRACT Fluorescence imaging in the second near‐infrared window (NIR‐II, 1000–1700 nm) has attracted increasing attention in biomedical applications owing to its deep tissue penetration, high spatial resolution, and low background autofluorescence. However, the rational optimization of high‐performance NIR‐II fluorophores remains challenging because of the complex relationship between molecular structure and optical properties. In this study, we integrated existing fluorescence datasets with NIR‐II fluorophore data to construct a comprehensive dataset covering maximum emission wavelengths from the visible region to the NIR‐II window. Based on this dataset, we developed a large language model (LLM)‐based framework for predicting molecular maximum emission wavelengths and compared its performance with conventional machine learning and deep learning models. The results demonstrated that the LLM achieved competitive predictive performance compared with the baseline models, highlighting the feasibility of LLM‐based structure–property prediction for fluorescent molecules. Model‐guided virtual screening was subsequently performed to prioritize candidate NIR‐II fluorophores, leading to the identification of two promising candidates that were experimentally characterized and exhibited favorable imaging performance in vitro and in vivo. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of LLM‐assisted structure–property prediction and virtual screening for NIR‐II fluorophores, providing an efficient computational strategy for candidate prioritization and molecular optimization.

This chapter examines how K-12 school leadership can convert artificial intelligence (AI) from a collection of tools into a governed programme of school improvement. It adopts an evidence-informed conceptual approach that integrates leadership theory, selected empirical research, and authoritative policy guidance on instructional use, administration, professional learning, decision-making, and ethical governance. No single leadership style is sufficient. Effective implementation depends on a configuration of transformational, digital instructional, distributed, adaptive, servant, ethical, and managerial functions, mediated by organisational AI readiness. The chapter differentiates low-, moderate-, high-risk, and normally prohibited applications; clarifies the human-AI division of labour; and connects leadership responsibilities with teaching, learning, assessment, operations, procurement, and stakeholder accountability.

Enhancing the agentic capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to tackle complex software engineering (SWE) and general terminal-usage problems is a pressing challenge. Current state-of-the-art LLMs often go through large-scale agentic Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, they mostly rely on high-level outcome rewards, with minimal consideration of low-level toolcall and mid-level workflow-stage rewards, which makes the training less effective. To overcome this limitation, we propose **Lean4AgenticRL**, which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first framework that grounds multi-level process rewards in the unified Lean4 formalization schema for open-ended agentic RL. **Lean4AgenticRL** first builds a *problem-specific workflow* system that balances the agent's own capability and controllability during execution, laying the foundation for further verification. Subsequently, our workflow formalization and multi-level reward annotation methods enable agent behavior verification within a general harness system. It provides multi-level rewards to support more effective agentic RL with the workflow-stage-normalized GRPO algorithm. Using **Lean4AgenticRL**, we train **LAR-9B/27B**, a family of models with enhanced agentic capability. Extensive experiments indicate that our model outperforms the leading model of similar size. **LAR-27B** achieves **77.3%** on TerminalBench-2.1. On average, our models outperform the base model by **9.89%** and surpass the second-best model of comparable size we know by **5.07%**. These results indicate the potential of integrating formal methods in enhancing open-ended agentic RL.

Learning from interaction experience is essential for enabling large language models to continually improve during deployment. Context distillation offers a promising path: privileged information extracted from experience is provided to a teacher, whose behavior is then distilled into a student model that has no access to it. However, both existing forms of context distillation have limitations. Off-policy context distillation trains the student on teacher-generated trajectories and thus suffers from exposure bias; whereas on-policy context distillation trains on the student's own rollouts, whose states are often uninformative and fail to convey behaviors the student cannot yet produce. To resolve this dilemma, we introduce Localized Context Distillation (LoCD). LoCD first localizes the critical spans of a student trajectory that require revision. The teacher then regenerates only these spans from the student's own prefix, and the student is trained on the regenerated segments. LoCD thereby concentrates learning on the most informative states while keeping exposure bias low. Extensive experiments across math reasoning, code generation, and agent tasks demonstrate that LoCD consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves more stable training with smaller and sparser parameter updates.

Background: Osteology classes provide students with the structural framework required for understanding normal anatomical relationships and subsequent clinical application. Despite repeated exposure to bones and anatomical specimens, students continue to make identification and relational errors. Conventional practical teaching emphasizes the recognition of correctly labeled structures, which may provide limited opportunities for students to actively identify, question and correct inaccurate interpretations. Error Embedded Education (EEE) is an educational strategy in which plausible anatomical errors are deliberately incorporated into learning materials, requiring learners to detect, classify, explain and correct the error. This approach may transform errors into active learning opportunities. Aim: To evaluate whether an osteology focused Error Embedded Education approach improves osteological reasoning and error detection ability among 1st year MBBS students compared with conventional osteology teaching. Methods: A prospective, randomized, controlled educational intervention was conducted among 83 1st year MBBS students. Participants were allocated to an Error Embedded Education group (EEE; n=42) and a conventional teaching control group (n=41). Both groups participated in eight weekly 60 minute osteology sessions using the same 10 specimens/images and equivalent instructional time. In the EEE group, realistic structural, positional/relational, variant versus anomaly, and developmental origin errors were deliberately embedded in specimens, images and case-based material. Students were required to identify, classify and correct the errors. The control group received the same specimens/images with correct conventional labeling. The primary outcome was the post module Osteological Reasoning Score (ORS). Secondary outcomes included Error Detection Sensitivity (EDS), 8 week retention of osteological reasoning, cognitive load and identification confidence. Between groups comparisons were performed using independent-samples t-tests, with ANCOVA used as a confirmatory analysis for the primary outcome. Effect sizes were expressed as Cohen's d, and Pearson correlation coefficients were used to explore relationships between selected outcomes. Results: The two groups were comparable at baseline with respect to age, sex, baseline osteological reasoning scores and previous osteology practical exposure. The mean post module ORS was significantly higher in the EEE group than in the control group (78.9 ± 7.6 vs. 70.2 ± 8.8; t=4.83, df=81; p<0.001; Cohen's d=1.06). Error detection sensitivity was also substantially higher among students receiving EEE (71.4 ± 11.2 vs. 52.7 ± 13.6; t=6.84, df=81; p<0.001; Cohen's d=1.50). At eight-week follow-up, the EEE group retained higher osteological reasoning scores than the control group (75.1 ± 8.0 vs. 64.3 ± 9.1; t=5.75, df=81; p<0.001; Cohen's d=1.26). Cognitive load was greater in the EEE group (58.3 ± 12.1 vs. 47.6 ± 11.4; Cohen's d=0.91), suggesting increased cognitive engagement during the intervention. Identification confidence was modestly but significantly higher in the EEE group (3.9 ± 0.6 vs. 3.6 ± 0.7; p=0.039; Cohen's d=0.46). Error detection performance varied according to error type: structural misidentification 82%, positional/relational 74%, variant versus anomaly 68%, and developmental origin errors 59%. Within the EEE group, in-module error-catching performance was positively correlated with post module ORS (r=0.52, p<0.001), whereas cognitive load was not significantly associated with post module ORS (r=0.11, p=0.47). Conclusion: Embedding realistic anatomical errors into osteology teaching significantly improved osteological reasoning, error-detection sensitivity and retention among first-year MBBS students compared with conventional correctly labeled teaching. Although EEE imposed greater cognitive demand, this additional effort was not associated with poorer learning outcomes and may represent productive cognitive engagement. Deliberate exposure to plausible errors, followed by explanation and correction, may therefore provide a useful educational strategy for developing more flexible and reflective anatomical reasoning. Keywords: Error Embedded Education, Osteology, Medical Education; Cognitive conflict, Anatomical Reasoning

This article reflects on our journey of working to facilitate discussions around the role of Generative AI (GenAI) in education within the Department of Media and Culture Studies (MCW) at Utrecht University during the academic year 2025–2026. What initially appeared to be a manageable question of GenAI’s impact on assessment and writing gradually revealed a complex web of concerns about student engagement, workloads, institutional priorities, and ultimately the purposes and values of higher education itself. Approaching the GenAI moment as a wicked problem, we realized we needed to shift our orientation from finding solutions to creating conditions for collective reflection, imagination, and experimentation. Ultimately, we suggest that responding to GenAI is not so much about finding a way out of uncertainty, but about learning to stay with it by remaining attentive to what emerges, creating space for what might become possible, and continuing to act from the anchor point of the educational purposes and values we care about.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. The steering agent observes the execution context, deciding when to intervene with a low-cost fast path and how to intervene with a high-cost slow path. To unlock its steering intelligence, the ability to assess goal drift and generate effective interventions, we jointly train the two paths with reinforcement learning, combining a pairwise ranking objective with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is now embedded in radiology workflows for prioritization, interpretation, quantification, and reporting. As adoption expands, radiologists must address professional responsibility, liability, patient disclosure, data governance, and algorithmic bias. This narrative review used PRISMA-informed, non-systematic methods. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched together with official regulatory and professional websites (including the World Health Organization, the Food and Drug Administration, the Department of Health and Human Services, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the European Commission, Indian Council of Medical Research, MeitY, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and AU/AUDA-NEPAD) for English-language literature and legal or policy documents published from January 2018 to March 2026. Search terms combined “radiology,” “artificial intelligence,” “ethics,” “liability,” “privacy,” “bias,” “governance,” “HIPAA,” “GDPR,” “DPDP,” and related terms. Review findings: global principles are converging, but implementation remains regionally contingent. We compare African, Asian, American, and selected international benchmarks, clarify that AFRI-CARE, ASIA-GUIDE, AMERICAS, and RADIANT are proposed conceptual frameworks, and show how they translate shared governance domains into practice. Defensible AI adoption in radiology requires transparent methods, local validation, subgroup monitoring, human oversight, and context-sensitive governance that reflects infrastructure, law, and equity priorities across regions.

Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical imaging and radiology research, improving image acquisition, interpretation, workflow efficiency, and decision support. However, its rapid adoption has introduced complex legal and regulatory challenges involving patient privacy, data governance, algorithm validation, liability, intellectual property, transparency, cybersecurity, and ethical oversight. A comprehensive understanding of the evolving legal landscape is essential for the safe, effective, and legally compliant implementation of AI in radiology. A narrative review of the published literature and current regulatory guidance was conducted. Relevant international legal and regulatory frameworks governing AI in medical imaging were evaluated, including the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, General Data Protection Regulation, U.S. Food and Drug Administration guidance on Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, World Health Organization recommendations, International Medical Device Regulators Forum principles, and selected national regulations. Key topics reviewed included data protection, informed consent, AI validation, regulatory approval pathways, post-market surveillance, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, explainability, and medico-legal responsibility. Current regulatory frameworks increasingly classify AI-enabled radiology software as SaMD, requiring risk-based evaluation, clinical validation, quality management systems, and continuous post-market performance monitoring. Regulatory authorities emphasize transparency, human oversight, data security, and lifecycle governance of AI systems. Nevertheless, important legal challenges remain, including liability for AI-assisted diagnostic errors, ownership of AI-generated outputs, secondary use of imaging data, cross-border data sharing, algorithmic bias, and regulation of adaptive or continuously learning AI models. The legal framework governing AI in radiology is evolving in parallel with technological innovation. Responsible integration of AI into clinical practice and research requires harmonized international regulations, robust data governance, standardized validation protocols, transparent algorithm development, and clearly defined legal accountability. Continued collaboration among radiologists, researchers, regulators, policymakers, industry, and legal experts will be essential to ensure that AI technologies remain safe, ethical, equitable, and trustworthy while maximizing their potential to improve patient care.
